series.name: Happier Times
series.tagline: Kuch log chale gaye. Kuch reh gaye. Kuch yaad reh gayi.
series.concept: A retired school principal passes away. His wife finds his diary — written over 20+ years. The audience reads along with her. Sir's house was where kids gathered — not formal tuition, a hangout where studying happened. Through diary entries, we trace what happened to each of these boys as life scattered them across the world.

episodes.title: The Diary

slides.text: He kept a diary. She never knew.
Three weeks after the funeral, she finally opened his cupboard. Old shirts, mothballs, a broken watch. And underneath everything — a diary. Brown. Worn. Pages yellow with age.

First page. No date. Just a list of names in his handwriting:

Rohit. Nikhil. Bunty. Omkar. Irfan.
Sagar. Vivek. Sachin. Mandar. Hemant.

She recognized two. Maybe three.

"Kaun the ye sab log?" she whispered.

They were the boys who used to fill this house. Who drank chai by the litre. Who called him 'Sir' even after they had children of their own.

Second page. A date: June 2003.

"Rohit came today. Thin boy, big eyes. Said his teacher-parents sent him. Asked if I could help with Maths. I said sit. He sat. He's still sitting."

She turned the page. Then another. Then another.

She didn't stop for three hours.

This is what she read.

Sir's diary, first line after the names:

"Mere apne bachche toh rahe nahi. Bhagwan ne doosron ke bheje. Main kya karta — darwaza band karta?"

episodes.synopsis: Sir's wife finds his diary while clearing his room after his passing. The first page has a list of names she barely recognizes. She begins to read.
episodes.caption:
He kept a diary for twenty years. She never knew.

Ten names on the first page. Ten boys who once filled a quiet house in a small town.

Do you remember the house where your group gathered? The one adult who let you all just... be?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The House on the Lane

slides.text: Every town has one house where kids just... end up.

Diary, August 2003:

"Galli mein sab kehte hain — Sir ka ghar. As if the house is mine. The house belongs to whoever walks in. I just pay the electricity bill."

One room. A long wooden table. Six chairs — later eight, later borrowed from neighbours. A blackboard Sir kept from his school days. A shelf of books nobody asked to borrow but everyone eventually did.

It wasn't tuition. Sir never charged a rupee. It wasn't coaching. He didn't follow any syllabus.

It was just a house where your marks didn't matter. Your father's salary didn't matter. You just had to show up.

5 PM: Boys arrive. Dump bags. Fight over chairs.
6 PM: Chai. Sir's wife made it without asking.
7 PM: Someone pretends to study. Others actually do.
8 PM: Sir says something nobody listens to.
9 PM: Everyone leaves. Sir smiles at the empty room.

Sir had two children once. Both lost to illness before they turned ten.

He never spoke of them. But the diary had a line:

"Ghar mein awaazein chahiye. Koi bhi ho. Bas khamoshi nahi."

Diary, December 2003:

"Ten boys now. The table is too small. The noise is too much. I haven't been this happy in years."

episodes.synopsis: Flashback through the diary: what Sir's house looked like, why kids started coming, how a retired principal's home became the one place in town where nothing mattered except showing up.
episodes.caption:
One room. One table. No fees. No syllabus. Just a retired principal who kept his door open because silence was worse than noise.

Did you have a place like this? Not home, not school — just somewhere you belonged?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The First Batch

slides.text: Five boys walked in that summer. Sir wrote about each one. He got almost everything wrong.

Diary, July 2003:

"Rohit — teacher parents, neat handwriting, always early. Sits in front. Will probably become a teacher himself."

He became a software engineer in Canada. Hasn't been home in three years.

"Nikhil — comes with Rohit. Doesn't say much. Doesn't study much either. But stays till the end. Something is there."

"Bunty — this one will either become something great or break three chairs. Today he broke one."
"Omkar — father is also a teacher. The boy says nothing but his notebook says everything. Every page filled. Every margin used. He will go far — if someone notices him."

"Irfan — came last. Didn't knock. Just walked in, sat down, solved the problem on the board that nobody could, and asked for chai.

This boy will either change the world or disappear from it. I don't know which worries me more."

Five boys. A teacher's son. A government clerk's son. A hyperactive dreamer. A silent grinder. A careless genius.

They had nothing in common. Except this room.

Diary, September 2003:

"Paanch ladke. Paanch duniya. Ek kamra.

Pehli baar laga — ghar phir se ghar lag raha hai."

episodes.synopsis: The seniors arrive at Sir's house — Rohit, Nikhil, Bunty, Omkar, and Irfan. Through diary entries, we meet each of them as 16-year-olds. Sir's first impressions, mostly wrong, mostly loving.
episodes.caption:
Five boys walked into a retired principal's house in 2003. A teacher's son, a clerk's son, a dreamer, a grinder, and a genius.

Sir wrote about each one. Got everything wrong. Got everything right.

Who were the five in your group? What would someone have written about you at sixteen?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Juniors

slides.text: A year later, five more showed up. The seniors weren't sure. Sir was.

Diary, June 2004:

"New boy. Sagar. Worn uniform, polished shoes. Scholarship student. Sat at the edge of the table — like he wasn't sure he deserved the full chair. He does."

"Vivek — father is the famous vakil. School chairman's son. Came in like he owned the place. Then touched my feet. Good boy hiding inside a loud one."

"Sachin — quiet. Reminds me of Omkar but warmer. Will never top an exam. Will top a life."

"Mandar — bank officer's son. Teachers' favourite already. Leaders mein se hai. But no one is guiding him. I must."

"Hemant — topped the school. Father passed last year. This boy carries more than his schoolbag. He laughs too much for someone carrying so much."

The seniors made them sit on the floor for a week. "Table pe baithne ka haq kamao."

Bunty enforced this. Irfan ignored it and gave Sagar his own chair on day two.

By day seven, everyone was on the floor. Including Sir.

Diary, August 2004:

"Das ladke ab. Table choti pad rahi hai. Awaaz zyada ho gayi hai. Chai ka kharcha double.

Koi baat nahi. Kharcha badhega toh badhne do."

"Seniors aur juniors mein farak sirf ek saal ka hai. Baaki sab — darr, sapne, confusion — bilkul same hai.

Bas seniors ko lagta hai unhe sab pata hai. Juniors ko lagta hai unhe kuch nahi pata.

Dono galat hain."

episodes.synopsis: Sagar, Vivek, Sachin, Mandar, and Hemant join Sir's house a year later. The senior-junior dynamic. The table gets louder. Sir watches two generations form one group.
episodes.caption:
Ten boys in one small room. Seniors who thought they knew everything. Juniors who thought they knew nothing.

Sir's diary: 'Dono galat hain.'

Remember when a one-year age gap felt like a generation? When did that change?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Equation

slides.text: Sometimes one person changes your life. They don't even know they did it.

Sagar couldn't solve it. Olympiad qualifier. Three weeks away. His school had no one to ask. His parents didn't know what an olympiad was.

He brought the paper to Sir's house like a patient bringing an X-ray to the wrong doctor.

Irfan glanced at the sheet. Didn't even pick it up.

"Number 4 mein sign change kar. Number 7 mein approach galat hai — integration nahi, series use kar. Baki sahi hai."

He went back to reading his novel.

Sagar stared at the sheet. All three were right.

For three weeks, Irfan taught Sagar. Not formally. Between cricket arguments and chai.

"Yeh dekh — isko aise soch. Pattern dekh. Problem nahi dekh, pattern dekh."

For Irfan, it was timepass. For Sagar, it was the first time someone treated his brain like it was worth investing in.

Sagar cleared the qualifier. State level.

Irfan shrugged. "Obviously."

Sir's diary: "Sagar came running today. Irfan didn't even look up. The boy who needed it most got it from the boy who valued it least. Life is strange like that."

That olympiad qualifier opened doors Sagar didn't know existed. Scholarships. Applications. A path out.

Years later, from a research lab in Germany, Sagar would tell people: "A boy I knew in 11th class changed my life in three weeks."

Irfan never knew. By then, Irfan was gone.

Diary, margin note, undated:

"Irfan ko pata nahi ki usne kya kiya. Shayad kabhi pata na chale.

Koi baat nahi. Achhe kaam ka receipt nahi milta. Bas asar dikhta hai."

episodes.synopsis: Irfan casually helps Sagar prepare for a math olympiad. For Irfan, it's Tuesday. For Sagar, it changes everything. Sir watches a genius unknowingly alter a life.
episodes.caption:
Irfan glanced at Sagar's math sheet for thirty seconds. Fixed three errors without picking it up. Went back to his novel.

Three weeks of casual tutoring later, Sagar cleared the olympiad. It changed his life. Irfan shrugged.

Who changed your trajectory without knowing it? Have you told them?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Scholarship

slides.text: His father did the right thing. Everyone said so. Except the boy who earned it.

Vivek's father was the kind of man the town introduced before itself. "Humara sheher? Haan, vakil sahab ka sheher."

School chairman. Respected. The kind of man who took cases for free when families couldn't pay. Good man. Generous man. Always thinking of others first.

Vivek got selected. Merit-based scholarship. Full tuition for college.

He ran home. First time in months he felt like something was his — not his father's, not the family's. His.

He told his father at dinner.

His father smiled. Hand on Vivek's shoulder.

"Beta, bahut achha kiya. Par humein zaroorat nahi hai. Yeh paisa kisi aur ke kaam aayega."

He meant it. He was thinking of someone else's son.

He wasn't thinking of his own.

Vivek told Sir the next day. Didn't cry. Didn't complain. Just said: "Papa ne mana kar diya."

Sir didn't say anything. Made him chai. Sat with him.

Sometimes the kindest thing is to not have an opinion.

Sagar — the scholarship kid — heard about it a week later.

He never mentioned it to Vivek. Never.

But something shifted. A boy whose family gave away what another family desperately needed — they understood each other differently after that.

Diary:

"Vivek ke papa ne scholarship lautwa di. Kisi aur ko mile, isliye. Achha socha. Sahi socha.

Par ladke ne mehnat ki thi. Uski mehnat ka jashn toh hona chahiye tha.

Achhe log bhi kabhi kabhi apne bachche ko bhool jaate hain."

episodes.synopsis: Vivek qualifies for a scholarship. His father — the town's renowned lawyer, school chairman — declines it. 'Someone else needs it more.' A kind decision. But Vivek's achievement goes uncelebrated. Sir's diary notes what gets lost when generosity forgets the boy standing right there.
episodes.caption:
Vivek earned a scholarship. His father returned it. 'Someone else needs it more.'

A kind decision. A generous one. But the boy who earned it — nobody celebrated him that day.

Has someone ever done the right thing... and you were the cost they didn't count?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: Bunty Being Bunty

slides.text: Every group has that one friend. The one who causes 80% of the chaos and 100% of the memories.

Bunty walked in with a plastic bag and a grin.

"Aaj padhai band. Movie night."

It was a Wednesday. Exams were in three weeks. Rohit said no. Nikhil said no. Irfan said "kaunsi film?" Bunty had already connected the DVD player to Sir's old TV.

The movie was terrible. Truly, genuinely, historically bad. Print was shaky. Audio was in the wrong language for twenty minutes. The plot made no sense.

Nobody moved for two hours.

They were laughing so hard the neighbours complained.

Sir walked in during the interval (Bunty had paused for chai, obviously).

He looked at the screen. Looked at the boys. Looked at the books gathering dust.

"Yeh kya chal raha hai?"

Then he pulled up a chair and watched the second half.

After the movie, nobody left. They made more chai. Bunty did impressions of every character. Irfan critiqued the physics of an action scene for forty minutes. Sagar laughed until he cried.

No studying happened.

Everything important did.

Three weeks later, everyone passed their exams.

Except Bunty. But that had nothing to do with the movie.

Diary:

"Bunty ne aaj poora ghar hila diya. Padhai zero. Masti hazaar.

Par sab ek saath hanse. Itni si baat hai. Itni si baat kaafi hai."

episodes.synopsis: Bunty — the kid who never studied but never missed a day — brings a pirated DVD for movie night. The movie is terrible. The evening is unforgettable. Sir pretends to be angry. He isn't.
episodes.caption:
Bunty brought a pirated DVD. The movie was terrible. The audio was wrong. The plot was nonsense.

Nobody moved for two hours. Sir pulled up a chair for the second half.

That's the thing about the best nights — you never plan them.

What's your group's 'worst movie, best night' story?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Topper

slides.text: The brightest boy in the room was also the one Sir worried about most.

Hemant's marks didn't make sense. Not for this town. Not for his school. 98, 97, 99, 96.

Teachers showed his papers to other students. Other parents asked his mother: "Kya karte ho?"

She didn't know. She was just trying to keep the lights on.

Hemant had a tongue like a razor. Funny, yes. But the kind of funny that left marks.

"Bunty, tu padh le warna tera dhaba mein kaam karega."

Everyone laughed. Even Bunty. Bunty now runs a dhaba. Hemant doesn't call him.

Sir saw it. The sarcasm wasn't confidence — it was a wall.

Hemant's father died when he was twelve. Heart attack. Standing in the kitchen. Hemant heard the fall.

After that, the boy decided: if you're the smartest person in the room, nobody asks how you feel.

One evening, after everyone left, Hemant stayed. Unusual.

Sir was cleaning the blackboard.

"Sir, mere papa ko heart attack aaya tha."

Sir stopped cleaning.

"Mujhe bhi aayega kya?"

Sir sat down. They talked until midnight. It was the only time Hemant wasn't performing.

Hemant would get into the best engineering college. Then the best MBA program. He would marry, divorce, earn well, spend little, call no one.

The armor held. But so did the loneliness underneath.

Diary:

"Hemant ka dimaag tez hai. Bahut tez. Par dil? Dil ko usne tala laga diya hai.

Ek din woh tala tootega. Mujhe darr hai ki tab koi paas nahi hoga."

episodes.synopsis: Hemant — fatherless, brilliant, sharp-tongued. He tops every exam but Sir sees something beneath the perfection: a boy using achievement as armor. Sir worries about what happens when the armor cracks.
episodes.caption:
Hemant topped every exam. Teachers showed his papers around. Parents asked his mother for secrets.

She was just trying to keep the lights on.

Sir's diary: 'This boy laughs too much for someone carrying so much.'

Do you know someone whose sharpness is just armor? Did anyone ever get through?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Full Table

slides.text: There was one evening when all ten were there. Nobody planned it. Nobody photographed it. But Sir wrote about it for two full pages.

March 2005. Load-shedding. One candle.

Rohit explaining trigonometry to Sachin. Irfan arguing with Hemant. Bunty arm-wrestling Nikhil. Omkar writing notes he'd keep for fifteen years. Sagar and Vivek quizzing each other. Mandar asking Sir about UPSC.

One candle. Ten boys. A lifetime.

"Chai khatam ho gayi."

Silence. Like someone announced a death.

Bunty: "Main bana leta hoon."

Everyone: "NAHI."

Sir's wife made another round. Twelve cups. Ten boys. One Sir. One wife who never complained.

Irfan said something about politics. Hemant disagreed. Nikhil took a side. Mandar tried to mediate. Bunty made it worse.

The argument lasted an hour. Nobody changed their mind. Nobody was angry.

That's what friendship is — fighting without consequence.

Around 10 PM, the argument died. Everyone was tired. Sprawled on chairs and floor.

Someone said: "Yaar, aisa hi rehna chahiye na. Sab saath."

Nobody answered. Because nobody disagreed.

Because nobody knew this was the last time all ten would be in one room.

They left in twos and threes. Rohit and Nikhil. Sagar and Vivek. Bunty alone, singing. Irfan and Hemant arguing still. Omkar, Sachin, Mandar — the quiet trio.

Sir stood at the door. Watched them walk down the lane. Waited until the last voice faded.

Diary, March 2005:

"Aaj sab the. Dasoan. Ek mombatti mein dasoan ke chehre dikh rahe the.

Mujhe pata hai yeh nahi rahega. Koi nahi rehta.

Par aaj — aaj bahut achha tha."

episodes.synopsis: A single evening when all ten boys are at Sir's house together. Studying, joking, fighting over chai, being young. This is the peak — the moment everything was complete. Sir's diary captures it like a photograph.
episodes.caption:
One candle. Ten boys. Load-shedding in a small town.

Someone said: 'Yaar, aisa hi rehna chahiye na. Sab saath.'

Nobody answered. Because nobody disagreed. And nobody knew it was the last time.

When was the last time your whole group was in one room? Did you know it was the last time?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: Things Sir Said

slides.text: Sir never gave speeches. He said small things. The kind you remember at 3 AM, fifteen years later.

To Rohit, when he worried about choosing the wrong career:

"Galat raasta koi nahi hota. Bas kuch raaste zyada lambe hote hain."

Rohit is in Canada now. Some days the road feels very long.

To Hemant, when he topped again:

"Marks se izzat milti hai. Izzat se pyaar nahi milta."

Hemant laughed. Twenty years later, divorced, alone in a Pune flat, he didn't.

To Bunty, when everyone mocked his marks:

"Duniya mein do tarah ke log hote hain — jo exam pass karte hain, aur jo log khush karte hain. Tu doosre type hai."

Bunty's dhaba is the happiest place in town.

To Sagar, when he worried about money:

"Paise ka tension sabko hai. Ameer ko bhi. Gareeb ko bhi. Farak sirf itna hai — ameer ko woh tension zyada dikhta hai.

Tu tension mat le. Tu kaam kar. Tension apne aap chala jayega."

It didn't. But the advice kept him moving.

And one entry that wasn't addressed to anyone:

"Main sirf chahta hoon ki yeh ladke achhe insaan banein. Marks aa jayenge. Job mil jayegi. Shaadi ho jayegi.

Par achha insaan? Woh banana padta hai. Roz. Poori zindagi."

None of the boys heard these entries.

None of them needed to.

Sir said the important things out loud. And wrote the rest where it mattered — for himself.

"Kuch baatein sunne ke liye nahi hoti. Likhne ke liye hoti hain."

episodes.synopsis: Small moments of Sir's wisdom — casual remarks, offhand advice, diary entries. Things the boys ignored at sixteen that would echo through their lives. Not grand speeches. Just quiet truths.
episodes.caption:
Sir never gave big speeches. He said things like:

'Galat raasta koi nahi hota. Bas kuch raaste zyada lambe hote hain.'

The boys didn't listen at sixteen. They hear him now, at thirty-five, alone in cities he never visited.

What's the one thing an elder told you that you only understood years later?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Borrowed Money

slides.text: It was two hundred rupees. It nearly killed a friendship.

Bunty needed money for something — he changed the reason every time he told the story. Nikhil lent it. No fuss.

"Laut de jab ho jaye."

That was October. By December, Bunty had spent it, forgotten it, and moved on.

Nikhil hadn't.

Nikhil didn't ask directly. He dropped hints. Then bigger hints. Then comments.

"Kuch logon ko yaad nahi rehta."

Bunty didn't get it. Or pretended not to. With Bunty, you never knew.

The room noticed. The room always notices before the people involved do.

It broke on a Thursday. Nikhil said something. Bunty said something back. Chairs scraped. Voices rose.

"Do sau rupaye ke liye itna drama?"
"Paisa nahi hai — izzat ki baat hai."

Bunty left. Didn't come for a week.

Nikhil stayed. But stopped laughing.

Sir was in the next room. Heard everything.

Rohit asked: "Sir, aap kuch boliye na."

Sir shook his head. "Yeh unka hai. Unhe solve karna padega. Main bol dunga toh woh seekhenge nahi."

It took two months. But they solved it.

Bunty came back. Put two hundred rupees on the table.

"Yeh le. Aur sun — main gadha hoon. Par tera gadha hoon."

Nikhil stared at the money. Then pushed it back.

"Rakh. Tujhe zyada zaroorat hai."

They never spoke about it again. That's how boys from small towns say sorry.

Diary:

"Bunty aur Nikhil ki ladai khatam. Do mahine lage. Koi maafi nahi maangi. Kisi ne nahi.

Par dono wapas aa gaye. Yehi maafi hai. Laut aana — yehi maafi hai."

episodes.synopsis: Bunty borrows money from Nikhil and doesn't return it. What starts as a small thing becomes a real rift. Sir sees it, understands it, but doesn't intervene. His diary explains why.
episodes.caption:
Two hundred rupees. Two months of silence. Zero apologies.

Bunty came back: 'Main gadha hoon. Par tera gadha hoon.'

Nikhil pushed the money back: 'Rakh. Tujhe zyada zaroorat hai.'

That's how boys from small towns say sorry. Has your group had a fight that ended without anyone actually saying sorry?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Last Week

slides.text: Nobody ever says "this is the last time." That's how last times work — you don't know until they're gone.

The room got quieter. Books replaced conversation. Chai went cold because nobody remembered to drink it.

The seniors had boards in two weeks. After that — college, jobs, cities, lives.

But nobody said that part out loud.

Two days before Rohit's first exam, he looked up and said:

"Yaar, exam ke baad sab milna. Pakka."

Everyone nodded. "Pakka. Hundred percent."

Sir's diary: "They all said pakka. It's the most common lie boys tell. Not to others — to themselves."

Irfan left first. Didn't announce it. Didn't do a round of goodbyes.

Just stopped coming one day. Left a note in the margin of Sagar's textbook:

"Pattern dekh, problem nahi. — I."

The last evening before exams was not dramatic. No speeches. No group photo.

Bunty complained about the syllabus. Sachin asked Rohit one last doubt. Omkar organized his notes. Hemant made a joke about failing.

Sir's wife made extra chai. As if more chai could make them stay.

They left one by one. "Kal milte hain" — but kal for some of them meant years.

Sagar and Vivek left last. Vivek turned at the gate: "Sir, hum aayenge."

Sir nodded. "Darwaza khula hai."

Diary:

"Kal se exams. Kal se yeh ladke bade hone lagenge.

Main rok nahi sakta. Koi nahi rok sakta.

Bas itna kahunga — happier times the. Bahut happier times the."

episodes.synopsis: 12th board exams approaching. The seniors are about to scatter. The last few days at Sir's house before everything changes. Nobody says goodbye because nobody believes it's really ending.
episodes.caption:
The last evening at Sir's house. No speeches. No group photo. Bunty complained. Sachin asked one more doubt. Sir's wife made extra chai.

'Kal milte hain,' they said. For some of them, kal meant years.

Sir's diary: 'Happier times the. Bahut happier times the.'

Did your group have a last evening? Or did it just... fade?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: Results Day

slides.text: Results day in a small town is a public event. Everyone knows before you do.

Hemant: first in the district. Obviously.
Rohit: decent. Good enough for engineering.
Omkar: quietly excellent.
Irfan: hadn't checked. Didn't care. Got 94%.

Sir's diary: "Four came running. Five phones rang. One didn't come and didn't call."

Bunty passed. Barely. Third division.

He didn't come to Sir's house that day. Or the next.

On the third day, Sir walked to Bunty's house. Sat with him. Said nothing for twenty minutes. Then: "Tu aayega kal?"

Bunty came.

The juniors watched the seniors' results like a preview of their own futures.

Sagar calculated what he needed to get a scholarship. Hemant's rank terrified Mandar. Vivek pretended not to care.

Bunty's result made everyone quiet. Not because they judged him. Because they saw themselves in what could happen.

Nikhil didn't do well. Not badly — but not enough for what he wanted.

He told no one. Just came to Sir's house, sat in his usual spot, opened a book.

Sir's diary: "Nikhil aaya. Kuch nahi bola. Kuch bolne ki zaroorat nahi thi. Main samajh gaya."

And just like that, results sorted them. Engineering. Commerce. Arts. Pune. Mumbai. Delhi. Nowhere yet.

The same table. The same chai. But now each boy had a different destination.

The scattering had begun. They just didn't call it that.

Diary:

"Results aa gaye. Kuch khush hain. Kuch nahi hain. Kuch samajh nahi pa rahe.

Mujhe sabse zyada uski chinta hai jo aaya nahi. Aur uski bhi, jo aaya par kuch nahi bola."

episodes.synopsis: Board results come. Some celebrations, some silence. Sir's diary captures who came to tell him their results, who didn't, and what the silence said.
episodes.caption:
Results day. The newspaper printed their names. The neighbours knew before the parents did.

Four came running to Sir. Five phones rang. One didn't come and didn't call.

Sir walked to that boy's house. Said nothing for twenty minutes. Then: 'Tu aayega kal?'

He came.

Do you remember who checked on you when results didn't go your way?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: See You Next Week

slides.text: The worst goodbyes are the ones that don't feel like goodbyes.

Rohit got placed. TCS. Pune first, then wherever.

The day he left, he came to Sir's house with sweets. Touched Sir's feet. Promised to call every week.

He called every week for three months. Then every month. Then Diwali. Then when he remembered.

Sir never once complained.

Irfan didn't say goodbye. To anyone.

One day his chair was empty. Sagar asked around. Someone said he'd left for college — top institution, somewhere in the south.

No farewell. No last chai. Just gone.

Sir's diary: "Irfan chala gaya. Pata nahi kisne bataya. Usne toh nahi."

Omkar left quietly. "Pune ja raha hoon. MTech milega dekhte hain."
Nikhil left loudly. "Boys, main wapas aaunga. Ruk." He didn't, for years.

Most goodbyes sounded like this: "Chal yaar, milte hain."

As if next week was guaranteed. As if distance was just geography.

Sagar walked Vivek home after the last senior left.

"Ab hum hain," Vivek said.
"Haan. Ab hum hain."

Two boys standing in a lane that felt twice as wide without the others.

Sir's house was the same. The table was the same. The chairs were the same.

But the sound was different. Less.

Sir kept the door open anyway.

Diary:

"Sab chale gaye. Koi 'alvida' nahi bola. Sab ne kaha 'milte hain.'

Shayad yehi theek hai. 'Alvida' mein finality hai.

'Milte hain' mein umeed hai. Jhoothi hi sahi."

episodes.synopsis: The seniors begin to leave. Rohit for his job, Irfan for college, others for their paths. Some goodbyes are grand. Most are casual — 'see you next week' — and then never. Sir records each departure.
episodes.caption:
Nobody said alvida. Everyone said 'milte hain.'

Rohit left with sweets and a promise to call weekly. Irfan just vanished. Omkar left quietly. Nikhil left loudly.

Sir kept the door open.

Did your group scatter all at once, or one by one? Which is worse?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Gap Year

slides.text: He got into a college. Just not the one he wanted. In a small town, that's the same as failing.

Vivek got into a law college. A decent one. But not NLS — the one he wanted.

He chose to wait a year and try again. In a town where gap years don't exist, choosing to wait looks exactly like failing.

Every uncle at the market: "Beta, is saal kya kar rahe ho?"

His father didn't know what to say. The man who argued cases for a living had no argument that could fix this.

He wanted to help. But how? He couldn't study for his son. He couldn't make a college say yes.

So dinner was quiet. Not angry. Just helpless.

Vivek came to Sir's house every day that year. Even though the seniors were gone. Even though most juniors were busy with their own 12th.

He studied law there. At the same table. In the same chair.

Sir never asked "kya hua." Just kept the chai coming.

Sagar called from wherever he could afford to. STD booth. Five rupees a minute.

"Padh raha hai?"
"Haan."
"Hoga is baar."
"Tu kaise jaanta hai?"
"Kyunki tu Vivek hai. Tujhe bas time lagta hai."

Five rupees well spent.

Vivek got in. Delhi. Law.

He told Sir first. Before his father.

"Sir, ho gaya."

Sir closed the diary he was writing in. "Mujhe pata tha."

Vivek cried. First time in that house. Last time too.

Diary:

"Vivek ka ho gaya. Ek saal laga. Sheher ne bahut kuch kaha.

Par ladka aaya. Roz aaya. Chup-chaap padha.

Jo roz aata hai, woh haar nahi sakta. Kabhi nahi."

episodes.synopsis: Vivek didn't get into his preferred law college. A year of waiting in a small town where everyone knows his father. The weight of a famous surname when you're struggling. Sagar and Sir are his anchors.
episodes.caption:
Vivek got into a college. Just not the one he wanted. He chose to wait a year and try again.

The town saw failure. He saw a decision.

He came to Sir's house every day. Sir never asked why. Just kept the chai coming.

He got in the second time. Told Sir before he told his father.

Have you ever made a choice that looked like failure to everyone except you?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Juniors' Turn

slides.text: Five chairs were empty. Five boys had to stop asking "Irfan hota toh?" and figure it out themselves.

The table had five empty chairs now. No Rohit to explain. No Irfan to show shortcuts. No Bunty to make them laugh.

Sagar sat where Irfan used to. Hemant took Rohit's spot. Nobody sat in Bunty's chair. It felt wrong.

Sir noticed.

Hemant studied like it was personal. Like each mark was a brick in a wall between him and his father's fate.

Top of every test. Every practice exam. Every mock.

Sir's diary: "Hemant ladh raha hai. Kis se, pata nahi. Shayad apne aap se."

Sagar needed a scholarship. Not wanted — needed. His family had calculated: if he scored above 90%, there was a chance. Below that, he'd work at the loom factory like his cousins.

Every mark was a rupee. Every exam was a door.

Mandar told Sir he wanted to be an IAS officer.

Sir looked at him a long time.

"Tu kar sakta hai. Par sun — UPSC sirf padhai nahi hai. Guidance chahiye. Woh tujhe yahan nahi milegi."

Mandar nodded. But where in this town would he find it?

And Sachin? Sachin studied. Not brilliantly. Not desperately. Just steadily.

Every day. Same time. Same pace.

Sir's diary: "Sachin se koi story nahi banti. Aur shayad yehi uski sabse badi takat hai."

Diary:

"Juniors ka boards. Sagar ko scholarship chahiye. Hemant ko first rank. Mandar ko UPSC ka sapna. Sachin ko bas stable life.

Sabki zaroorat alag hai. Par darr sabka same hai."

episodes.synopsis: Sagar, Hemant, Sachin, Mandar, and Vivek (now gone) — the remaining juniors face their own boards. The house is emptier. The stakes feel personal. Sir notices who has changed.
episodes.caption:
The seniors left footprints. The juniors had to find their own path.

Sagar needed marks to escape the loom factory. Hemant studied like each mark was armor. Mandar dreamed of UPSC. Sachin just showed up, every day.

Sir's diary: 'Everyone's need is different. But the fear is the same.'

What were you fighting for in 12th? Did you even know?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Crossroads

slides.text: Some dreams die not from lack of talent but from lack of a map.

Mandar wanted to be a collector. He'd seen one visit his school once — the way the crowd parted, the way his father straightened his shirt.

"Yeh banna hai," he told Sir.

At sixteen, it sounded like destiny. At twenty, it sounded like stubbornness. At twenty-four, it sounded like a prayer.

The town had no UPSC coaching. The nearest was Pune — four hours, fees his bank-officer father couldn't afford.

Mandar studied from library books. Photocopied notes. Second-hand guides.

He was running a marathon in slippers while others had running shoes.

First attempt: prelims cleared. Mains failed.
Second: mains cleared. Interview failed.
Third: missed prelims by two marks.
Fourth: didn't clear.

Four years. Four attempts. Each one closer and further at the same time.

The town stopped asking. His father stopped hoping. Mandar stopped telling people.

At twenty-five, Mandar took an IT job in Pune. The salary was decent. The work was fine.

"Fine" is the saddest word for someone who wanted to be extraordinary.

He never talked about UPSC again. Changed the subject when anyone brought it up.

Sir's diary, years later, after a call from Vivek:

"Vivek batata hai Mandar Pune mein hai. IT job. Theek hai.

Par agar koi usse coaching deta... agar koi batata kaise karna hai... woh collector hota.

Mujhse nahi hua. Meri bhi galti hai."

"Mandar mein sab tha. Dimaag tha. Mehnat thi. Irada tha.

Raasta nahi tha.

Duniya mein kitne Mandar hain? Kitne raaste nahi milte?

Main soch ke thak jaata hoon."

episodes.synopsis: Mandar's UPSC dream versus his reality. No coaching, no mentors, no roadmap. A small-town boy with a big dream and nobody to show the way. Sir sees the gap between potential and access.
episodes.caption:
Mandar wanted to be a collector. Four UPSC attempts. No coaching. No guidance. No map.

He took an IT job in Pune. 'Fine' — the saddest word for someone who wanted extraordinary.

Sir blamed himself: 'Mujhse nahi hua. Meri bhi galti hai.'

Do you know a Mandar? Someone who had everything except the path?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Quiet House

slides.text: A house doesn't get quiet all at once. It happens one empty chair at a time.

2007: Sagar left for research. "Sir, Germany ja raha hoon."
2007: Hemant left for engineering college. Didn't say where.
2008: Sachin went to Pune. Quiet as always.
2008: Mandar started UPSC prep. Alone.

Vivek was in Delhi. He called sometimes.

Diary entries from 2009-2012:

"Rohit called. Canada mein hai. Thak gaya lagta hai."
"Nikhil ka phone aaya. Kuch nahi kaha. Bas sun raha tha."
"Vivek aaya. Bahut din baad. Achha laga."
"Irfan ka koi haal nahi. Koi nahi jaanta."

Four years in four lines.

Sir's wife would sometimes set out extra chai cups. Habit. Then she'd put them back.

"Koi nahi aaya aaj?"
"Nahi."
"Kal aayenge."
"Haan. Kal aayenge."

Kal never came. But they kept saying it.

Sir kept the door open. Every evening. 5 PM.

Sometimes a neighbourhood kid wandered in. Sir gave them chai. Showed them a math trick. They left.

They weren't the same. Nothing was the same.

But the door was open. Always.

Diary, 2013:

"Aaj kisi ne phone nahi kiya."

Just that. Nothing else on the page.

Diary, later:

"Ghar wahi hai. Darwaza wahi hai. Chai wahi hai.

Bas awaazein chali gayin.

Par main intezaar karunga. Koi toh aayega. Koi toh."

episodes.synopsis: Sir's house empties. The juniors have left too. Diary entries become shorter — fragments, dates, silences. Sir keeps the door open but the footsteps have stopped.
episodes.caption:
2013. Sir's diary had one line:

'Aaj kisi ne phone nahi kiya.' Nobody called today.

The house was the same. The door was the same. The chai was the same. Only the voices had gone.

But Sir kept the door open. Every evening. Five PM.

When was the last time you called someone who's waiting?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: Ten Thousand Miles

slides.text: Rohit left to build a life. He built a career instead. He didn't notice the difference for years.

TCS. Then another company. Then another. Pune to Bangalore to Toronto.

Each move was a promotion. Each promotion was a distance.

Rohit's apartment in Canada had everything. Except noise. Except mess. Except ten boys arguing about cricket.

Rohit called Sir every few months.

"Sir, Nikhil kaisa hai? Sagar ka kya hua? Bunty ka dhaba chal raha hai?"

Sir would ask: "Tu kaisa hai?"

"Main theek hoon, Sir. Achha hoon."

Sir's diary: "Rohit kehta hai achha hai. Achha hota toh 11 baje raat ko phone nahi karta."

Rohit's mother passed in 2019. Heart. Like all things in that family — sudden and quiet.

He couldn't get a flight in time. COVID visas. Paperwork. By the time he landed, she was ash.

The boy who promised to call every week hadn't visited in three years.

He came back for the rituals. Sat in his parents' house. Neighbours came.

"Canada mein bahut achha kar raha hai."

Rohit wanted to scream: I missed my mother's funeral. What part of this is achha?

He didn't scream. He served tea. That's what the eldest son does.

Before leaving again, Rohit went to Sir's house. Sat in his old chair. Didn't speak for an hour.

Then: "Sir, main galat jagah hoon. Par wapas aane ki himmat nahi hai."

Sir held his hand. "Himmat baad mein aa jayegi. Pehle rona aane de."

Diary:

"Rohit aaya. Canada se. Bahut door se.

Par asli door toh woh apne aap se tha.

Bada ho gaya hai. Par andar wahi ladka hai. Dara hua. Akela."

episodes.synopsis: Rohit's life in Canada — corporate job, loneliness abroad, the guilt of missing things back home. His phone calls to Sir where he asks about everyone but reveals nothing about himself.
episodes.caption:
Rohit went to Canada. Built a career. Missed his mother's funeral.

He went to Sir's house before leaving again. Sat in his old chair. 'Sir, main galat jagah hoon. Par wapas aane ki himmat nahi hai.'

Sir held his hand: 'Pehle rona aane de.'

Have you ever been too far from the right place and too scared to go back?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Lab

slides.text: Sagar escaped the loom factory. He didn't escape the math. Every rupee still counted.

The scholarship boy got a scholarship. Then another. Then a PhD position in Germany.

His mother cried at the airport. Happy tears. Proud tears.

Sagar cried on the plane. Different tears. The kind nobody talks about — leaving home when home is all you have.

His PhD advisor was brilliant and brutal. Published everything. Cared about nothing.

"Your work is not good enough. Do it again."

Sagar did it again. And again. For two years.

He sounded tired on the phone. Sir noticed. Sir always noticed.

Sagar switched labs. Lost two years. Started over.

In India, two years is an engineering degree. Abroad, it's a line on your CV that says "didn't work out."

He didn't tell his mother. He told Vivek. Vivek told Sir.

Germany paid him. Not a lot, but more than his father ever earned.

Sagar still ate the cheapest bread. Still walked instead of taking the tram. Still sent money home.

You can leave poverty. Poverty doesn't leave you.

Vivek sent a voice note at 2 AM India time. He'd been drinking. Old Monk probably.

"Sagar, tu yaad hai na? Teri jagah khali hai. Yahan bhi. Sir ke ghar bhi. Jaldi aa."

Sagar saved that voice note. He still has it.

Diary:

"Sagar Germany mein hai. Bahut mushkil mein tha. Phir se shuru kiya.

Yeh ladka girta hai aur uthta hai. Baar baar.

Usse rokna possible nahi hai. Yeh mujhe yakeen hai."

episodes.synopsis: Sagar's research life in Germany — a bad PhD advisor, restarting, still counting every rupee despite earning. The scholarship boy who made it out but found that 'out' has its own cages.
episodes.caption:
Sagar escaped the loom factory. PhD in Germany. Bad advisor. Two lost years. Started over.

Still ate the cheapest bread. Still sent money home.

Sir's diary: 'This boy falls and gets up. Again and again. Stopping him isn't possible.'

Do you know someone who kept getting up? Tell them today.

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Vanishing

slides.text: Some people don't leave your life. They leave the world you understand.

Irfan was always going somewhere nobody could follow.

Top college — nobody from the town had gotten in before. Then Oxford offered him a PhD. Full funding. The town celebrated.

Irfan said no.

The town stopped understanding.

He went to Turkey. Theology. Islamic studies. Nobody knew why. Nobody dared ask.

Sir's diary: "Irfan Turkey gaya. Oxford chhod diya. Log kehte hain pagal hai. Main kehta hoon — shayad wahi akela sachchi cheez dhoondh raha hai."

Irfan rose. Became someone in those circles. Married. Divorced. Married again.

Irfan called Sir once. 2015. From somewhere in the Middle East.

"Sir, main theek hoon. Bas... sab bhool gaye honge."
"Koi nahi bhoola, Irfan."

A long pause.

"Sagar ko mera salaam."

Then the line went dead. He never called again.

Sagar tried. For years. Emails bounced. Numbers disconnected. LinkedIn profile deleted.

Someone said they'd seen Irfan in Riyadh. Someone else said Doha. A cousin said he's fine, leave him alone.

The boy who solved equations nobody else could had become an equation nobody could solve.

Irfan left behind a note in Sagar's textbook.

"Pattern dekh, problem nahi."

That's what remains of a genius — a scrawl in a margin. And a boy in Germany who became a researcher because of it.

Diary, final entry about Irfan:

"Irfan ka pata nahi. Kahan hai, kaise hai, kya kar raha hai.

Bas itna jaanta hoon — jahan bhi hai, woh sabse tez hai.

Aur sabse akela bhi."

episodes.synopsis: Irfan's trajectory — brilliant, mischievous, top college, Oxford PhD offer, then theology in Turkey, rising in religious ranks, Middle East, two marriages, and then... silence. Sir's diary tracks the vanishing.
episodes.caption:
Irfan said no to Oxford. Went to Turkey. Rose in theological circles. Married twice.

Called Sir once in 2015: 'Sab bhool gaye honge.' Sir said: 'Koi nahi bhoola.'

Then silence. For good.

The smartest boy in the room became someone nobody could find.

Do you have an Irfan? Someone who just... vanished?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Crack

slides.text: Hemant did everything right on paper. Paper doesn't know how to cry.

Top engineering college. First class with distinction.
Top MBA. Campus placement. Big salary.

Every step looked like success from outside. From inside, each step was further from anyone who knew the boy without the armor.

He married a colleague. Smart, accomplished, like him.

Two ambitious people in one house is a corporation, not a home.

It lasted four years. No children. No scenes. Just two people who forgot to be anything other than successful.

The divorce was as efficient as everything else in Hemant's life.

After the divorce, the sarcasm got sharper. Every message was a joke. Every call deflected.

"Tum sab ki shaadi chal rahi hai? Meri nahi chali. Par mera EMI toh chalu hai. Priorities."

Nobody laughed. Hemant laughed for everyone.

He stopped calling Sir. Stopped calling anyone.

Nikhil tried: "Chal milte hain." No reply.
Rohit tried from Canada. Voicemail.
Sagar sent a long email. Read receipt. No response.

The padlock Sir worried about twenty years ago — it had finally closed.

Sir's diary, 2018:

"Hemant ka koi phone nahi aaya. Vivek batata hai woh Pune mein hai. Theek hai. Akela hai.

Mainne kaha tha — ek din tala tootega aur koi nahi hoga.

Woh din aa gaya."

"Hemant — tujhe koi sun nahi sakta. Kyunki tune darwaza band kar diya.

Par main yahan hoon. Darwaza khula hai.

Bas aana hai."

episodes.synopsis: Hemant's adult life — top engineering college, top MBA, but the armor of achievement begins to crack. Failed marriage, tight with money, sarcasm as shield, stops calling anyone. Sir's worst fear comes true.
episodes.caption:
Hemant did everything right on paper. Top college. Top MBA. Marriage.

The marriage lasted four years. The sarcasm got sharper. The calls stopped.

Sir wrote directly to him in the diary — something he never did for anyone else:

'Darwaza khula hai. Bas aana hai.'

Hemant never came.

Is there someone you've stopped reaching out to? Or someone who's stopped reaching you?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Quiet Ones

slides.text: Nobody will make a reel about Sachin. Nobody will write a thread about Omkar. That's exactly why Sir did.

Sachin got a job. Then a promotion. Then a flat in Pune.

No headline. No drama. Just one foot in front of the other for fifteen years.

Sir's diary: "Sachin — no story. And maybe that IS the story. The boy who never broke, never soared, just kept going."

Omkar went to Germany for MTech. Came back. Started a small consulting firm in the hometown.

People said: "Germany se aake yahan? Pagal hai."

Omkar didn't explain. He never did. He just worked.

The firm is doing well now. Omkar still says nothing.

Mandar codes in Pune. Goes home on weekends. Plays cricket with local boys.

Sometimes, late at night, he opens the UPSC syllabus PDF. Scrolls through it. Closes it.

A dream he visits like a grave — with respect, with sadness, never for too long.

Vivek was the thread. He visited Sir. Gave updates.

"Sachin bought a flat. Sachin got married. Sachin's wife is nice."
"Omkar's firm got a government contract."
"Mandar is... Mandar. Theek hai."

Three boys reduced to status updates. Three lives richer than any summary.

Diary:

"Sachin, Omkar, Mandar — teenon ke baare mein likhne ko zyada nahi hai. Koi badi udaan nahi. Koi bada tootna nahi.

Par teenon zinda hain. Apne tarike se. Apni jagah pe.

Shayad yehi kaafi hai. Shayad hamesha se yehi kaafi tha."

"Duniya Hemant aur Irfan ki kahaniyaan sunegi. Rohit aur Sagar ke baare mein poochegi.

Par Sachin, Omkar, Mandar — inke baare mein koi nahi poochega.

Isiliye main likh raha hoon. Kisi ko toh yaad rakhna chahiye."

episodes.synopsis: Sachin steady in Pune, Omkar consulting from hometown, Mandar in IT. No drama. Small updates via Vivek. The lives that don't make stories but make the world work.
episodes.caption:
Sachin bought a flat. Omkar built a firm. Mandar opens the UPSC syllabus at night sometimes, then closes it.

No headlines. No drama. Just three boys who became three men who kept going.

Sir: 'Nobody will ask about them. That's why I'm writing. Someone should remember.'

Who are the quiet ones in your group? Have you checked on them lately?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The One Who Stayed

slides.text: Everyone left to find themselves. Vivek found himself by staying.

Delhi law school done. Big firm offers in Mumbai and Delhi.

Vivek came back. To the town. To the lane. To the practice.

"Papa ke baad kaun sambhalega?" he told Sagar.

Sagar knew that wasn't the whole reason. The whole reason was sitting at a table, keeping a door open.

Vivek built a practice. Not his father's — his own. Land disputes, family law, small cases.

The people who once pitied his gap year now came to him with their problems.

The chairman's son who couldn't leave became the town's most needed man.

Every Sunday. 5 PM. Vivek at Sir's door.

Chai. The same table. Updates about everyone.

Sir lived for Sundays. Vivek knew this. That's why he never missed.

Vivek was the bridge. He told Sir about Rohit's Canada, Sagar's Germany, Bunty's dhaba, Nikhil's struggles.

Sir's diary was mostly Vivek's updates by now:

"Vivek aaya. Bataya ki Sagar ka paper publish hua. Achha laga. Bahut achha laga."

Sagar called Vivek every week. They talked like no distance existed.

"Yaar, tu rehne de. Tune toh life sort kar li."
"Sort nahi ki. Bas ghar aa gaya."
"Wohi toh. Sort."

Diary:

"Sab gaye. Vivek reh gaya.

Log poochhte hain kyun nahi gaya. Main jaanta hoon.

Kyunki isko pata hai ki ghar kya hota hai. Isko pata hai ki log kya hote hain.

Yehi sabse badi samajhdaari hai."

episodes.synopsis: Vivek returns to the hometown after law school. Becomes the town's top lawyer. He's the only one who visits Sir regularly. The rich boy who chose to stay.
episodes.caption:
Everyone left. Vivek came back.

Every Sunday, five PM — chai with Sir. Updates about every boy who'd scattered.

Sir's diary: 'People ask why he didn't leave. I know why. Because he knows what home means.'

Who's the Vivek in your group? The one who stayed? Have you thanked them?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Second Fall

slides.text: Nikhil fell twice. The first time, nobody noticed. The second time, the world was falling too.

Let me tell you about Nikhil's rise first.

Bad 12th marks. Everyone wrote him off. Then MTech from a top college. Then DRDO. Defence research. Cutting edge.

The late bloomer bloomed. Spectacularly.

Sir called him one of his proudest moments.

COVID hit. Contracts cut. Nikhil — contract employee, not permanent — was out.

Ten years of proving himself. Gone in one email.

"Due to restructuring, your position..."

He read it three times. Then called Rohit. Then Sir.

"Sir, phir se wahi jagah pe hoon. Shuru se."

"Tujhe yaad hai pehli baar kya hua tha?"

"Haan. MTech mila."

"Toh is baar bhi kuch milega. Tu late bloomer hai. Late. Bloomer nahi chhod."

Nikhil laughed. First time in weeks.

Rohit sent money from Canada. "Bhai, rakh. No arguments."
Vivek found him legal freelance work.
Bunty sent food from the dhaba. "Khana kha. Baaki baad mein."

The group that had scattered — they didn't come back together. But they reached out. In their own ways. From their own distances.

Nikhil found work. Took time. Wasn't DRDO. Wasn't cutting edge.

But it was a floor to stand on. And Nikhil knew about floors — he'd been on them before.

Late. But blooming.

Diary:

"Nikhil phir gira. Phir utha.

Yeh ladka tootne ke liye nahi bana.

Aur is baar — uske dost the. Door se. Par the."

episodes.synopsis: Nikhil — the late bloomer who made it to DRDO — gets laid off during COVID. The fighter gets hit again. But this time, the group shows up differently.
episodes.caption:
Nikhil fell once. Nobody noticed. He got up — MTech, DRDO, cutting edge.

COVID pushed him down again. This time, from different cities and countries, the group reached out.

Sir told him: 'Tu late bloomer hai. Late. Bloomer nahi chhod.'

Who caught you when you fell the second time?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Dhaba

slides.text: The kid who never passed an exam became the only one who passed the test that matters — are people happy to see you?

After 12th, Bunty tried everything. Sales. Driving. A brief terrible attempt at a call center.

Nothing stuck. He was too loud for offices, too restless for routines.

Then his uncle's dhaba came up for sale. Bunty borrowed money — not from Nikhil this time — and bought it.

Bunty's dhaba is not fancy. Plastic chairs. Tin roof. No menu — he tells you what's good today.

But the food is honest. The chai is endless. And Bunty is at every table, talking, laughing, making everyone feel like the only customer.

Hemant said he'd end up here. He was right. He just didn't know it would be the happiest ending.

Sir came once. With his wife. Sat at a corner table.

Bunty saw him. Left everything. Personally made him chai. Served him himself.

"Sir, aapka paisa nahi lagega. Kabhi nahi."

Sir tasted the chai. Smiled.

"Achhi chai banata hai tu. Padhai se better."

When Nikhil lost his job, Bunty sent food. Every day. For three months.

The boy who once borrowed two hundred rupees and almost broke a friendship — he now fed his friend without being asked.

He never mentioned the two hundred rupees. Neither did Nikhil.

Some debts don't need repaying. They need surpassing.

Bunty will never be rich. He'll never leave the town. He'll never have a degree on the wall.

But at 8 PM every night, his dhaba is full. People are laughing. Chai is flowing.

Sir was right: "Tu doosre type hai." The type that makes people happy.

Diary:

"Bunty ka dhaba dekha. Bahut achha chal raha hai.

Sabse kam padha hua ladka. Sabse zyada khush.

Zindagi ka mazaak nahi hai yeh. Zindagi ka sabak hai.

Khush karna bhi ek talent hai. Aur Bunty ke paas hai."

episodes.synopsis: Bunty — the kid who never opened a book — runs the most popular dhaba in town. Life's punchline. But also life's kindest surprise.
episodes.caption:
The boy who never opened a book runs the most popular place in town.

When Nikhil lost his job, Bunty sent food for three months. The boy who once borrowed two hundred rupees now feeds without being asked.

Sir's diary: 'Sabse kam padha. Sabse zyada khush. Yeh zindagi ka sabak hai.'

Success doesn't always look like what we expected, does it?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Handwriting Changes

slides.text: You can read a man's health in his handwriting. Sir's started trembling in 2023.

2022: Monthly entries.
2023: Every few months.
2024: Two entries. January. And one in March.

The diary was going quiet. Like the house before it.

Diary, January 2024:

"Doctor ne kaha rest karo. Main poochta hoon — kisse? Ghar mein do log hain. Main aur woh. Chai banati hai. Main peeta hoon. Bas.

Kabhi kabhi Vivek aata hai. Tab awaaz aati hai."

Diary, February 2024:

"Kuch baatein kehni thi jo nahi kahi. Irfan ko — tujhe rokna chahiye tha. Hemant ko — darwaza khol. Mandar ko — maaf kar mujhe, main coaching nahi dila paya.

Rohit ko — ghar aa. Sagar ko — thak mat."

Same page, different ink — he came back to it:

"Par proud bhi hoon. Sachin ki stability. Bunty ki khushi. Omkar ka ghar wapas aana. Nikhil ka uthna. Vivek ka rehna.

Aur Sagar — uss ladke ne pattern dekh liya. Irfan theek keh raha tha."

She watched him write. Slower now. His hand sometimes stopping mid-word.

"Kya likh rahe ho?"
"Kuch nahi. Yaadein."

She didn't read the diary then. She wishes she had.

She's reading it now.

Diary, March 2024:

"Haath kaamp raha hai. Likhna mushkil ho raha hai.

Par main likhunga. Jab tak likh sakta hoon.

Yeh ladke meri zindagi the. Inhe bhoolna nahi hai. Kisi ko nahi bhoolna hai."

episodes.synopsis: Sir's health declines. Diary entries become sparse, shaky. He writes about what he's proud of, what he wishes he'd said. The handwriting itself tells the story.
episodes.caption:
The handwriting changed in 2023. Steadier hands had written about five boys arriving in 2003. Now the same hands trembled writing about the men they'd become.

Sir wrote his regrets and his pride. The regrets shook. The pride steadied his hand.

'Yeh ladke meri zindagi the. Inhe bhoolna nahi hai.'

Who's writing your story while you're not looking?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Last Calls

slides.text: Sir made three phone calls. Each one a goodbye. Nobody knew except him.

Rohit called on a Tuesday. 11 PM Indian time. As usual.

"Sir, kaise hain aap?"
"Theek hoon. Tu bata."

They talked for an hour. Sir asked about Canada, about work, about whether he'd eaten.

At the end: "Rohit — tu achha ladka hai. Hamesha tha."

Rohit laughed. "Sir, aap filmy ho rahe ho."

Sir laughed too. Put the phone down. Cried.

Vivek came Sunday. As always.

Sir was in bed — "Thoda thhak gaya." Vivek brought chai to the bed.

They talked about everything. Sagar's latest paper. Bunty's new dish. Nikhil's new job.

Sir held Vivek's hand at the end. "Tu ruka. Sabse badi baat yeh hai."

Vivek didn't understand then. He does now.

Nikhil called Wednesday. Excited about his new project.

Sir listened. Laughed at the right places. Asked questions he already knew answers to — just to keep Nikhil talking.

"Sir, main phir se khada ho gaya."
"Mujhe pata tha. Tujhe pata nahi tha. Wohi farak hai."

He didn't tell any of them.

Not Rohit. Not Vivek. Not Nikhil.

His wife asked: "Unhe bata do."

"Kyun? Woh aayenge. Chinta karenge. Rone lagenge. Mujhe woh sab nahi chahiye.

Mujhe bas unki awaaz chahiye. Khush awaaz. Bus."

Diary, his last week:

"Teenon se baat hui. Rohit, Vivek, Nikhil.

Baaki se nahi ho payi. Koi baat nahi.

Jinse baat hui, unhe pata nahi ki yeh aakhri thi.

Achha hi hai. Alvida mein bahut weight hota hai. Normal mein nahi. Normal rehne do."

"Maine teenon ko woh baat kahi jo kehni thi. Bina bataye ki yeh aakhri hai.

Rohit — tu achha hai.
Nikhil — main jaanta tha.
Vivek — tu ruka.

Yehi kaafi hai. Zindagi bhar ke liye yehi kaafi hai."

episodes.synopsis: Rohit calls from Canada. Vivek visits. Nikhil calls. Sir talks to them normally — doesn't tell them he's unwell. Each call is a quiet goodbye that only Sir knows is a goodbye.
episodes.caption:
Sir called them. Rohit, Vivek, Nikhil. Talked normally. Laughed at the right places.

His wife said: 'Tell them.'

'Nahi. Mujhe bas unki khush awaaz chahiye.'

He said what needed to be said. Without them knowing it was the last time.

Have you said what needs to be said? Or are you waiting for a better time that may not come?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Last Page

slides.text: The first page had their names. So did the last.

The morning of the last entry. Sir sat at the study table. The same table. First time in months.

His wife helped him to the chair.

"Yahan kyun?"
"Likhna hai."
"Bistar pe likh lo."
"Nahi. Yahan likhna hai. Isi table pe."

He opened the diary to the next blank page.

Took a long time. His hands were shaking. The pen felt heavy.

But he wrote. Slowly. Carefully. Like the first entry — deliberate, loving, certain.

The last entry:

"Aaj phir yaad aaye. Sab.

Rohit, Nikhil, Bunty, Omkar, Irfan.
Sagar, Vivek, Sachin, Mandar, Hemant.

Das ladke. Das duniya. Ek kamra.

Maine kuch nahi kiya. Darwaza khola. Chai di. Baithne diya.

Baaki inhone khud kiya. Achha kiya. Bura kiya. Par kiya.

Mere achhe bachche the. Hain. Rahenge."

He put the pen down. Closed the diary.

Looked at the room. The table. The chairs.

Smiled.

Then his wife helped him back to bed.

The study room. Empty again. The diary on the table. The pen beside it.

Chairs for ten. A table with chai stains from decades.

A blackboard with nothing on it. And everything on it.

The door — still open.

"Mere achhe bachche the.

Hain.

Rahenge."

episodes.synopsis: Sir's final diary entry. Simple. Maybe just a line. Maybe just their names again. The beginning and the end are the same — a list of names from someone who loved them.
episodes.caption:
The last diary entry. The same ten names from the first page.

'Maine kuch nahi kiya. Darwaza khola. Chai di. Baithne diya.'

'Mere achhe bachche the. Hain. Rahenge.'

They were. They are. They will be.

Who's been quietly holding the door open for you?

#HappierTimes #SirKeBachche #SmallTownStories

episodes.title: The Group

slides.text: Sir left. His diary stayed. His wife sent a photo to the only place all ten still existed — the WhatsApp group.

She didn't know what to say. So she took a photo of the first page.

Ten names in his handwriting.

Sent it to the group Vivek had made years ago. The group where only birthday wishes survived.

Caption: "Yeh mila unke cupboard mein. Aap logon ke naam hain."

The group exploded.

Rohit: "Sir..." Nikhil: "Kya. Kab." Bunty: voice note — just crying. Sagar: a long message, middle of the night, Germany time.

Hemant appeared online. Typed. Stopped. Typed. Stopped. Finally: "Sir ke jaisa koi nahi tha."

Irfan: nothing. But he was online. For four minutes.

For three hours, the group was alive. Really alive.

Remembering the movie night. The chair Bunty broke. The chai that ran out. Irfan's blackboard trick. Hemant's one-liners. Sir's advice that nobody heard and everyone remembers.

For one evening, they were sixteen again. In one room. At one table.

By midnight, the messages slowed. People had to work. Sleep. Live.

By morning, the group was quiet again.

By afternoon, life had resumed.

The grief was real. The silence after was also real.

Both are love.

Three weeks later, a notification:

"Happy Birthday Nikhil! 🎂"
— Sachin.

Then Rohit: "HBD bhai!"

Then Bunty: voice note singing happy birthday, badly.

Life went on. Not because they forgot Sir. But because Sir would have wanted the chai to keep flowing.

The diary is closed. Sir's voice is gone.

But somewhere in a small town, the door is still open.

And somewhere, in a group of ten scattered men, a voice note is playing.

Bunty, singing happy birthday.

Badly.

Beautifully.

— Happier Times.

episodes.synopsis: Sir passes. His wife sends a photo of the diary's first page to the boys' WhatsApp group. It lights up. For one evening, memories pour in. Then silence. Then a birthday wish three weeks later. Life.
episodes.caption:
Sir left. His wife found the diary. Sent a photo of the first page to the WhatsApp group.

The group exploded. For one evening, they were sixteen again.

Three weeks later: 'Happy Birthday Nikhil 🎂' — Sachin.

Bunty sent a voice note. Singing. Badly. Beautifully.

The diary is closed. The door is still open.

— Happier Times.
